patent: Boeing patent (inventors Biornstad, Blankinship, George and Ingram). Provisional filed 2004-04-06, application filed 2004-05-20, issued 2009-05-05, certificate of correction 2018-10-16. It describes a fuselage section built as one composite shell running 360 degrees about its axis. The background sets this against the honeycomb sandwich shells of the Raytheon Premier I and Hawker Horizon, and against fuselage halves or quarter-panels joined along longitudinal seams. Stiffeners sit in grooves of a rotating tool, tows or tape go on over them, and the two are cocured in an autoclave. A second idea concerns the frame joint: stiffener flanges reach toward each other to form a nearly continuous surface, so the frame needs no joggles. Claim 34 recites a one-piece barrel with a cross-sectional dimension of at least 12 feet; claim 35 adds a skin with no longitudinal joint. The patent names no Boeing aircraft. CompositesWorld describes Spirit AeroSystems' 787 fuselage section as a one-piece barrel made by fiber/tape placement with co-cured stringers, but no source found says this patent covers those barrels. US 8,182,628 is in the same family.

glossary.def: A closed fuselage shell segment, joined to its neighbors at circumferential joints.
Untwisted bundle of continuous fibers, here supplied impregnated with resin.
Fiber already impregnated with partly reacted resin; the patent writes "preimpregnated". Stays tacky until cured.
Automated lay-up in which a head collimates several prepreg tows, presses them on with a roller, and can cut and restart each tow.
Automated lay-up of wider prepreg tape. Common usage now reserves it for flat or gently curved parts and uses fiber placement on complex contours, unlike the wording at col. 2 line 48.
Continuous fiber wound under tension onto a rotating mandrel, without the cut and restart of fiber placement.
Form that sets the inner shape of the part during lay-up. The tool assembly 700 serves this role.
Curing two uncured parts together so the resin itself forms the bond, as opposed to secondary bonding of a cured part with adhesive.
Longitudinal stiffener with a closed-top hat cross-section and two flat flanges. Aircraft usage often says stringer.
Circumferential ring stiffener that keeps the fuselage shape and crosses the stringers.
Cutout in a frame that lets a stringer pass through.
Small step formed in a part so it can pass over another part's edge.
Extra local material added to carry load across a joint or around a feature.
Through-thickness tension that lifts a bonded flange off a skin; bonded joints are weak in it.
Circumferential tension in the shell, chiefly from cabin pressure.
Plate laid on a laminate under the bag to spread pressure and give a smooth surface.
Sealed film over a lay-up; evacuating it presses the plies together and removes trapped air.
Heated pressure vessel for curing. 350 F is the usual cure temperature for aerospace epoxy.
Low-expansion iron-nickel alloy used for tooling because its thermal expansion is close to carbon fiber laminate.
Ultrasonic check in which one transducer sends a pulse and reads reflections from voids or disbonds.
Locating parts by features or holes in the parts themselves rather than by hard fixtures.
